# Writing your own functions {#sec-own-functions}

Sooner or later every analysis needs a calculation that no package provides — an
index from a paper, a data check specific to your field protocol, a summary your lab
always reports. This chapter is about turning that calculation into a function that
is easy to call, hard to misuse, documented and tested.

@sec-functions introduced the syntax. Here the focus is on what makes a function
good: sensible arguments, clear errors, a docstring, and tests that tell you when you
break it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this chapter comes from

This chapter and @sec-resampling are **inspired by** the programming and resampling
modules of **ecoR** [@oliveira_ecor], the R course wiki of the Instituto de
Biociências, Universidade de São Paulo, produced and maintained by Alexandre Adalardo
de Oliveira. The idea of building ecological indices as functions, step by step, comes
from there. The text, examples and exercises here are written from scratch for Julia;
the authors of ecoR have not reviewed this book.

If you read Portuguese and want to go further, the original material is freely

## From a calculation to a function {#sec-fn-calculation}

Suppose you want to know how variable richness is across ponds, relative to its mean.
The coefficient of variation answers that, and it is one line:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-inline
std(ponds.richness) / mean(ponds.richness) * 100
```

The moment you want it for a second variable, or per region, the line becomes a
function. Give it a name that says what it computes, and the argument a name that says
what it expects:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-function
cv(x) = std(x) / mean(x) * 100

cv(ponds.richness), cv(ponds.body_size)
```

Richness varies far more, relative to its mean, than body size does.

A function can return several things at once. The idiomatic way is a **named tuple**,
whose fields you read by name:

```{julia}
#| label: named-tuple
count_summary(x) = (n = length(x), mean = mean(x), var = var(x))

s = count_summary(ponds.richness)
s.mean, s.var
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.1 — Variance-to-mean ratio

For counts, the variance-to-mean ratio says how individuals — or species — are spread
across sampling units. If the counts follow a Poisson distribution, variance equals the
mean and the ratio is about 1; above 1 the counts are more clumped, below 1 more even.
Write `vmr(x)` and check it with `check("10.1", vmr)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Same shape as `cv`: one line, `var` over `mean`. `var` is the sample variance, which
divides by $n - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-1
vmr(x) = var(x) / mean(x)

vmr(ponds.richness)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-1-check
check("10.1", vmr)
```

Richness across all 180 ponds has a ratio of about 3.3: far more variable than a
Poisson with a single mean. That does not yet mean the counting process is odd — the
ponds differ in area, canopy and region. @sec-fn-groups returns to this.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-1
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.1", vmr)
```

## Arguments: defaults and keywords {#sec-fn-arguments}

A function often has a sensible default that the user may want to change. `cv` returns
a percentage; someone might prefer a proportion. There are two ways to offer that.

A **positional argument with a default** comes after the others and is set by
position:

```{julia}
#| label: positional-default
cv_pos(x, percent = true) = std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1)

cv_pos(ponds.richness), cv_pos(ponds.richness, false)
```

A **keyword argument** goes after a semicolon and is always set by name:

```{julia}
#| label: keyword
cv_kw(x; percent = true) = std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1)

cv_kw(ponds.richness; percent = false)
```

For options like this, keywords are the better choice: `cv_kw(x; percent = false)`
says what it does, while `cv_pos(x, false)` makes the reader look up what `false`
means.

A function can also collect keywords it does not know and pass them on with
`kwargs...`. Here `rounded_cv` handles `digits` itself and hands everything else to
`cv_kw`:

```{julia}
#| label: kwargs-forward
rounded_cv(x; digits = 1, kwargs...) = round(cv_kw(x; kwargs...); digits)

rounded_cv(ponds.richness), rounded_cv(ponds.richness; percent = false, digits = 3)
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

R has one kind of argument, which can be given by position or by name. Julia separates
them: arguments before the `;` are positional, those after are keywords and must be
named. `kwargs...` plays the role of R's `...` when forwarding options to another
function.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.2 — Standardizing, with options

Write `standardize(x; center = true, scale = true)`. By default it returns
$(x - \bar x) / s$; `center = false` skips subtracting the mean and `scale = false`
skips dividing by the standard deviation. Check it with `check("10.2", standardize)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Build the result in two steps, each depending on its option:
`centered = center ? x .- mean(x) : x`, then divide `centered` by `std(x)` only if
`scale` is true.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-2
function standardize(x; center = true, scale = true)
    centered = center ? x .- mean(x) : x
    return scale ? centered ./ std(x) : centered
end

check("10.2", standardize)
```

`std(x)` is computed on the original `x`, so it is the same whether or not you center.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-2
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.2", standardize)
```

## Refusing bad input {#sec-fn-errors}

A function that quietly returns nonsense is worse than one that stops. `cv` has two
blind spots:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-nonsense
cv([0, 0, 0]), cv([-5, 5])
```

`NaN` for an empty pond survey, and an infinite coefficient for data with a negative
value, which counts cannot have. Checks at the top of the function catch both, and
`throw(ArgumentError(...))` tells the caller that the problem is the input, not the
function:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-checked
function cv_checked(x)
    any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("values must be non-negative"))
    mean(x) > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the CV is undefined"))
    return std(x) / mean(x) * 100
end

try
    cv_checked([-5, 5])
catch e
    e
end
```

The `condition && action` form reads as "if condition, then action"; `condition ||
action` as "unless condition, action". Both are idiomatic for checks like these.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `@assert` is for your own mistakes

`@assert condition` stops when something that should never happen does. Use it to
check your own reasoning inside a function; use `ArgumentError` for input that a user
could plausibly get wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.3 — A safer `vmr`

Rewrite `vmr` so that it throws an `ArgumentError` when it gets fewer than two values,
any negative value, or a mean of zero, and still returns the ratio otherwise. Check it
with `check("10.3", vmr)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Three checks, one line each, before the calculation. `length(x) < 2`,
`any(<(0), x)` and `mean(x) == 0` are the conditions.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-3
function vmr(x)
    length(x) < 2 && throw(ArgumentError("need at least two values"))
    any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("counts cannot be negative"))
    mean(x) == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the ratio is undefined"))
    return var(x) / mean(x)
end

check("10.3", vmr)
```

This replaces the one-line `vmr` from 10.1: a method with the same argument types
overwrites the old one.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-3
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.3", vmr)
```

## Documenting a function {#sec-fn-docs}

A string placed immediately before a function becomes its **docstring**, which is
what `?cv_documented` shows in the REPL and what VS Code shows when you hover over the
name. The convention is the signature indented by four spaces, then one or two
sentences on what the function does and returns:

```{julia}
#| label: docstring
"""
    cv_documented(x; percent = true)

Coefficient of variation of `x`: the standard deviation divided by the mean,
times 100 unless `percent = false`. Throws an `ArgumentError` if the mean is zero.
"""
function cv_documented(x; percent = true)
    mean(x) > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the CV is undefined"))
    return std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1)
end
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

Docstrings play the role of `roxygen2` comments, with one difference: they are part
of the language, available as soon as the function is defined, with no build step.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.4 — Document `vmr`

Add a docstring to your `vmr` from 10.3: the signature, what the ratio means, and which
inputs it refuses. Run the definition again and try `?vmr` in the REPL. Then check it
with `check("10.4", vmr)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

The docstring goes directly above `function vmr(x)`, with nothing in between —
not even a blank line.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-4
"""
    vmr(x)

Variance-to-mean ratio of the counts `x`. About 1 for Poisson counts, above 1 when
counts are clumped, below 1 when they are more even. Throws an `ArgumentError` for
fewer than two values, negative values, or a zero mean.
"""
function vmr(x)
    length(x) < 2 && throw(ArgumentError("need at least two values"))
    any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("counts cannot be negative"))
    mean(x) == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the ratio is undefined"))
    return var(x) / mean(x)
end

check("10.4", vmr)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-4
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.4", vmr)
```

## Your function, per group {#sec-fn-groups}

A function you write works inside a Tidier pipeline — with one catch. Tidier knows
that `mean`, `std` or `sum` summarize a whole column, but it does not know that about
your `cv`. By default it applies unknown functions to **each value separately**, which
here would compute a coefficient of variation for every single pond:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-per-region-wrong
wrong = @chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(cv_richness = cv(richness))
end

nrow(wrong), first(wrong.cv_richness, 3)
```

180 rows of `NaN` instead of three numbers, and no error. Putting `~` in front of the
function tells Tidier to pass it the whole column:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-per-region
@chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(cv_richness = ~cv(richness), cv_body = ~cv(body_size))
end
```

The same with `DataFrames.jl` directly (@sec-native-dataframes), where the question
does not arise:

```{julia}
#| label: cv-per-region-native
combine(groupby(ponds, :region), :richness => cv => :cv_richness)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check the number of rows

After `@summarize`, you should have one row per group. If you have one row per
observation, Tidier has applied your function to each value: add the `~`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.5 — Is richness clumped within regions?

Compute the variance-to-mean ratio of `richness` for each region, in a column called
`vmr`, using your function. Check it with `check("10.5", by_region)`. Are the ratios
closer to 1 than the value for all ponds together?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

The `~cv` block of this section, with `~vmr` in place of `~cv`. Without the `~`, your
`vmr` from 10.3 receives one pond at a time and rightly refuses it: "need at least two
values".
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-5
by_region = @chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(vmr = ~vmr(richness))
end

check("10.5", by_region)
```

The ratios, from about 1.8 to 3.2, are all lower than for the pooled ponds (3.3):
part of the variation came from differences between regions. They are still above 1,
because ponds within a region differ in area and canopy. In @sec-overdispersion a
Poisson model that accounts for these predictors had no overdispersion left. A ratio
above 1 in raw counts is a reason to look for predictors, not proof that the counts
are not Poisson.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-5
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.5", by_region)
```

## Functions that take functions {#sec-fn-higher-order}

In Julia, functions are values: they can be stored in a vector, passed to another
function, or written without a name. That makes it easy to apply several summaries at
once:

```{julia}
#| label: several-summaries
[f(ponds.richness) for f in (mean, median, cv, vmr)]
```

An **anonymous function** is written `x -> expression`. `map` applies one to every
element of a collection — here, to three columns of the data:

```{julia}
#| label: anonymous
map(col -> round(cv(col); digits = 1), eachcol(ponds[:, [:area_m2, :temp_c, :body_size]]))
```

Area varies enormously between ponds, temperature very little: the coefficient of
variation puts variables with different units on the same scale.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 10.6 — Morisita's index

Morisita's index of dispersion compares how often two individuals picked at random
fall in the same sampling unit with what a random spread would give:

$$
I_d = n \, \frac{\sum_i x_i (x_i - 1)}{N (N - 1)}
$$

where $x_i$ is the count in unit $i$, $n$ the number of units and $N = \sum_i x_i$.
It is about 1 for a random spread and above 1 for a clumped one. Write
`morisita(x)`, check it with `check("10.6", morisita)`, and apply it to these counts of
tadpole clusters in ten quadrats along a pond margin:

```{julia}
#| label: data-10-6
quadrats = [0, 3, 0, 0, 7, 1, 0, 0, 5, 0]
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`x .* (x .- 1)` gives $x_i(x_i - 1)$ for every unit at once; `sum` adds them up.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-6
function morisita(x)
    N = sum(x)
    return length(x) * sum(x .* (x .- 1)) / (N * (N - 1))
end

morisita(quadrats)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-10-6-check
check("10.6", morisita)
```

About 2.8: the clusters are strongly clumped, in three of the ten quadrats. A version
for real use would refuse `N < 2`, as in 10.3.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-10-6
#| include: false
Checks.verify("10.6", morisita)
```

## Testing your functions {#sec-fn-tests}

`check` has been testing your functions against inputs whose answers are known. You
can do the same for your own functions with the `Test` standard library, and rerun the
tests every time you change the code:

```{julia}
#| label: testset
@testset "cv_checked" begin
    @test cv_checked([10, 10, 10]) == 0          # no variation
    @test cv_checked([1, 2, 3]) ≈ 50             # std 1, mean 2
    @test_throws ArgumentError cv_checked([0, 0])
    @test_throws ArgumentError cv_checked([-1, 1])
end;
```

Good tests use cases you can work out by hand, and include the inputs the function
should refuse. Type `≈` as `\approx` followed by `Tab`; it compares floating-point
numbers with a tolerance, where `==` would fail over rounding.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where your functions should live

Once a function is useful beyond one script, move it to a file of its own — say
`functions.jl` in your project folder — and load it with `include("functions.jl")` at
the top of each analysis. The tests can live in a second file next to it. When the
collection grows, the next step is a package, which `Pkg` can create for you with
`Pkg.generate`.
:::

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. Write a `@testset` for your `morisita` with cases you can compute by hand: all
   individuals in one unit, and exactly one individual per unit. What should each
   give?
2. Add a `Matrix` method to `vmr` (@sec-dispatch) that returns one ratio per column,
   treating each column as a species counted across quadrats (rows).
3. `cv` fails on a column with missing values, such as `canopy`. Add a keyword
   `skipmissing = false` that, when true, ignores them. Which default is safer, and why?
